title: Getting started
text: Getting started Bairava is an experimental 2D engine written in Zig. The repository includes a small sample game that imports the engine through its supported game-facing module, @import("bairava") . Requirements - The Zig version pinned in build.zig.zon ( 0.16.0-dev.3142+5ccfeb926 for this checkout). - Slang's slangc compiler on PATH . - Internet access for the first build so Zig can fetch the pinned dependencies. Build and run the sample From the repository root: The sample is compiled by the normal build graph and installed at zig-out/bin/BairavaSample . It demonstrates a game that imports only bairava , configures the engine, loads a texture, draws through a SpriteBatch , maps physical controls to game actions, and switches between scenes. Use zig build to build Semkootru, the repository's larger sample game. Explore the public API Start with the generated [public API reference](../api/). The [sample source](https://github.com/ash5me/Bairava-Engine/tree/main/sample) is the runnable example for lifecycle, drawing, input, assets, entities, and scenes. Other guides in this site cover specific subsystems and their current limits. The API is in early development and is not production-ready. Do not treat internal engine modules as stable game interfaces; game code should import the named bairava module.

title: Application lifecycle
text: Application lifecycle Game code imports the bairava module and gives bairava.run a game type and a bairava.Config . The engine validates configuration before opening platform resources, creates the context, calls the game's init , and then repeats fixed-step update and per-frame draw until the game stops. Compile-checked public API example This headless example is compiled and run by zig build test ; the normal zig build also compiles the public-API sample game. Lifetime and failure behavior - The allocator in Config must outlive the complete run call. - A successful game init is paired with game teardown before GPU and platform teardown. - If game init returns an error, game teardown is not called. Release resources acquired before the failing operation inside init . - The context passed to init and update is borrowed for that call. Do not retain it. - Updates use the configured fixed frequency. Drawing happens once per presented frame and is not a fixed-step callback. Config.validate can be used to report invalid values before calling run . Startup errors are returned to the caller; a clean stop returns normally. The run contract is also summarized in the [public API reference](../api/). Run the sample game From the repository root, zig build run-sample builds and launches the scene sample. It uses the public API and requires a display and a supported SDL GPU device.

title: Assets and resource ownership
text: Assets and resource ownership Asset paths passed to Context are relative to the executable's packaged asset directory. Use loadTexture , loadAtlas , and the corresponding typed loaders for packaged resources; recover from their returned errors instead of assuming files exist. Textures loadTexture returns an owned texture value. Deinitialize it before the run ends, normally from the owning scene's teardown. For name-registered textures, acquireTexture returns a counted handle: balance each successful acquire or retain with releaseTexture . A released or unloaded handle is invalid and may produce HandleError . The resource cache can unload idle entries to honor its configured budget. A handle is not a promise that a GPU allocation can never be evicted; request or resolve the resource through its documented context operations. Build-time asset validation Use the asset manifest and the asset validation guides to check packaged files before runtime. zig build check-assets validates repository asset metadata and generated atlas indexes. Asset source files and packaged files have different roles; only files included by the manifest are available to the running game. Threading Background workers can decode staged data, but GPU upload and renderer operations remain on the engine thread. Any allocator used by worker-visible work must be safe for the configured worker count. Set worker threads to zero when deterministic main-thread work is more important than parallel decoding.

title: Input and action mapping
text: Input and action mapping Poll input through the Context passed to update . Bind physical controls to a game-owned enum so gameplay responds to actions such as jump rather than to a particular key. Define defaults The compile-checked [public API example](application-lifecycle.html) defines a typed action enum, default key bindings, and an action map without requiring a window or graphics device. ActionMap accepts keyboard, mouse, gamepad button, and gamepad-axis bindings. An action can have up to four default bindings. Exceeding that limit is a programmer error; the settings reader reports and drops excess configured bindings. Read input during update - held stays true while any binding is down. - pressed and released are one-update-step edges; do not expect an edge to persist into a later update. - value returns a normalized strength, useful for analog sticks and triggers. - Read the state during update ; drawing is not the input-consumption phase. The optional settings file can override defaults using bairava.bindings . Bindings are SDL-free public values, so the same action can work across keyboard and gamepad controls.

title: Rendering sprites and cameras
text: Rendering sprites and cameras Rendering is submitted from the game's draw callback through the frame's DrawContext.batch . The renderer owns the frame target and submission lifecycle; game code does not initialize or flush the batch directly. World and screen coordinates The camera and sprite rectangles use pixel-valued world coordinates. DrawContext.cam converts world positions into the current view. Use its conversion methods when placing a sprite in world space; screen-space UI can instead use the view layout. The configured native view is a reference size, not a crop that changes with window aspect ratio. The view is fitted into the window using the configured scale mode. Query the layout rather than assuming that window points and world pixels are interchangeable, especially for mouse input. Submission and order - Load a texture during initialization or update, then submit it during draw . - drawSprite takes a source rectangle in texture texels and a destination rectangle in view pixels. - Use SpriteOptions.z for depth ordering and preserve meaningful submission order for equal depth. - Keep the DrawContext and references to its frame-scoped data inside the callback. - Keep GPU operations on the engine thread. The public [sample game](https://github.com/ash5me/Bairava-Engine/tree/main/sample) shows camera conversion, sprite submission, tinting, and parallax. It is compiled by the normal build. Backend limits SDL GPU is the feature-complete renderer. The SDL3 2D renderer option is reserved and resolves to SDL GPU until the alternate path is implemented. Renderer capability queries are runtime information; do not infer support from a requested configuration alone.

title: Scenes and transitions
text: Scenes and transitions Use SceneHost(RootScene) to run a scene stack with bairava.run . A scene owns its state and resources; the navigator is borrowed only during update . A scene supplies: - init(ctx) !Self to construct it. - update(self, ctx, nav) to update and request a transition. - draw(self, dc) to submit frame drawing. - deinit(self) or the context-aware teardown hook when resource release needs the context. switchTo , push , and pop are applied after the current scene's update returns. A newly requested scene is not updated in the middle of the caller's update. If initialization of a transition fails, the open scenes remain active and the error is logged. Do not retain ctx , dc , or nav past the callback. A successful scene initialization is paired with teardown when it is replaced, popped, or the host shuts down. The repository's [public-API scene sample](https://github.com/ash5me/Bairava-Engine/tree/main/sample) is compiled by the normal build and demonstrates the complete lifecycle.

title: Behavior trees
text: Behavior trees The engine exposes engine.ai , a small allocation-free behavior-tree runtime for game-independent decisions. A tree is defined as a flat []const ai.Node ; composites refer to child nodes by u16 index. ai.Node.run(action) creates an action, while ai.Node.sequence(children) and ai.Node.selector(children) create composites. Actions receive a caller-owned context as anyopaque and return ai.Status.success , .failure , or .running . A sequence succeeds only when all children succeed, and fails on the first failure. A selector succeeds on the first success, and fails only when every child fails. Both composites stop on .running and resume at that child on the next tick. reset clears those cursors so evaluation starts over. The tree validates that all nodes are reachable from its root, child references are in range, and the graph is a tree rather than a cycle or shared-child graph. The node array, child-index slices, and anything captured by action callbacks must outlive the tree. The sample game's enemy uses a small dedicated state machine; the generic behavior tree is available to games that need reusable sequence/selector composition. Navigation primitives and the navigation.Agent that combines route planning with movement are documented in [navigation](navigation.html).

title: Animation data
text: Animation data The engine parses and advances animation clips without SDL. A clip is a row of frames with durations. The animation machine chooses which clip plays, from parameters the game sets each update. Frame rectangles, timing, and the choice of clip are data, so gameplay code only says what the entity is doing. Clip format, version 1 Each frame rectangle is relative to the source texture region and measured in texels. Durations are positive seconds. clip names may contain lowercase letters, digits, and underscores. Each clip must have at least one frame. loop wraps to its first frame; once holds the last frame. Every frame line gives x y width height duration ; rectangles must be non-empty and fit entirely within the source region. Blank lines and comments are ignored. Unsupported versions, duplicate clip names, malformed or non-positive frame durations, and out-of-bounds rectangles are rejected with parse errors. engine.animation.Library.parse validates and owns the parsed definition; find returns stable clip references until deinit , and indexOf returns the clip's index. Animation machine, version 1 The machine is text too. It names parameters, states, the clips each state can play, transitions between states, and frame events. A parameter is an integer that the game sets. A trigger parameter is cleared when a transition that tests it fires, so it acts once. - A state plays its first clip variant whose condition holds. If none holds, it plays its first variant. A variant with no when always holds. A state holds up to four variants. - A condition is param OP value , where OP is == , != , , or = . A bare param means param != 0 . Join conditions with and ; a clause holds up to four. - A transition is transition FROM - TO , with optional when , blend SECONDS , and event NAME , in that order. FROM may be , which matches any state. Transitions are tried in the order written, and at most one fires per update. A transition into the current state never fires. - blend crossfades the clip being left over the given seconds. A transition with no blend switches at once. Variant changes inside a state never blend; they restart the clip. - event STATE FRAME NAME emits NAME when playback reaches FRAME in that state. Frame events fire as playback passes a frame, so a clip that starts on a frame does not emit that frame's event until it wraps or moves past it. An update that passes a whole loop of a short clip may emit fewer events than the frames it passed. - A state frame event or transition event may use a string name or a decimal integer ID. Integer IDs are stored in FrameEvent.id or the transition's event id ; pollEvent() exposes both name and id . - The start state is the first state, unless a start line names another. - machine.stateName() , clipName() , clipTime() , and frameIndex() report the current position. - machine.pose() returns the frame to draw. While a blend runs it also returns the frame of the clip being left, and the weight of the current frame. Draw the old frame fully, then the new one at its weight. - machine.pollEvent() returns queued events, oldest first. Sixteen events can wait; more are dropped and counted in dropped . - machine.restore(library, elapsed) settles the state from the current parameters, seeks the clip, and blends nothing and queues no events. Games use it when loading a save. machine.hooks is a fixed four-slot listener list. subscribe(context, callback) returns false when full; subscribing the same callback and context twice keeps one slot. unsubscribe(context, callback) removes a slot without changing the order of the rest. Hooks receive HookNotice values for authored events and blend started , blend finished , and blend interrupted phases. They are separate from pollEvent() : authored event hooks still fire when the poll queue is full, and blend phases never enter that queue. A transition that interrupts a blend reports the interruption, then any new blend start, then its authored event. Restore and instant settling are silent. Callback name slices remain borrowed from the machine definition or clip library. Callbacks may use set , but must not call update , restore , deinit , pollEvent , subscribe , or unsubscribe on the machine. engine.animation.MachineDefinition.parse checks the text against a library. Unknown clips, parameters, and states, malformed lines, and too many items are parse errors. The definition copies its text, so the library may be replaced without invalidating it, but the clip indices must still match that library. The warrior The sample warrior's clips are in [ assets/animations/warrior.anim ](https://github.com/ash5me/Bairava-Engine/blob/main/assets/animations/warrior.anim), and its machine is [ assets/animations/warrior.machine ](https://github.com/ash5me/Bairava-Engine/blob/main/assets/animations/warrior.machine). The machine has moving and facing parameters, with facing 0 down, 1 right, 2 up, and 3 left, so it chooses the idle or walk clip for each direction. The game sets those two parameters each update and does not name clips. It checks the frame rectangles against the warrior atlas region at startup, and the machine checks its clip names when it loads. zig build test covers parsing, rectangle bounds, looping metadata, variable frame durations, deterministic advancement, machine transitions, blending, variants, triggers, events, and restore. Skeleton data, version 1 A skeleton is a hierarchy of bones with sprites attached to them, and animations that key each bone's position, rotation, and scale. Like clip data, it is text that starts with a version header. engine.animation.skeleton.Data.parse validates it against the size of its source region before any of it is used, and deinit releases the result. Fields are separated by spaces or tabs. Blank lines and lines that start with are ignored. Readers reject any other version. bone NAME PARENT X Y ROTATION SCALE declares a bone. The first bone is the root, and its parent is - . Every other bone names an earlier bone as its parent. Position is relative to the parent, rotation is in radians and turns clockwise on screen, and scale is a uniform factor greater than zero. A skeleton holds at most 64 bones. attach BONE X Y W H OFFSET X OFFSET Y PIVOT X PIVOT Y draws one sprite on a bone. X, Y, W, and H give its rectangle in texels, relative to the source region, and the rectangle must lie inside that region. The offset places the pivot in the bone's space. The pivot is the point inside the sprite that sits on that spot, and the sprite turns around it, so it must lie inside the rectangle. Attachments draw in the order they are listed. anim NAME loop once LENGTH starts an animation whose length is in seconds. Every bone and attach line comes before the first anim . event TIME NAME OR ID adds a marker to the current animation. Event times must be in increasing order and lie from zero through the animation length. String names use lowercase letters, digits, and underscores; a decimal integer is accepted as an event ID. Player.pollEvent() returns Event { name, id } : string events keep id == null , while integer-only events keep an empty name. key BONE rotate scale TIME VALUE and key BONE translate TIME X Y add keys. A rotate or scale key replaces the bone's rotation or scale, and a translate key replaces its position. The keys of one property on one bone must be listed together, in increasing time order, and they must lie within the animation's length. A bone and property that appears again after another track in the same animation is an error. A scale key must be greater than zero. Evaluation is in engine.animation.skeleton.evaluate(&data, animation, time, &pose) . It writes every bone's world transform to a Pose without allocating. Keys interpolate linearly. A looping animation wraps its time, and between its last key and its first key it interpolates across the wrap. A one-shot holds its first key until that key's time, and its last key after the end. A property with no keys keeps its rest value. A child is placed in its parent's rotated and scaled space, and it inherits the parent's rotation and scale. skeleton.Player plays one animation. It holds a pointer to the data, the animation, and a time, and it offers init , play , update(dt) , finished , and pose . pollEvent() returns crossed event markers in playback order. Up to 16 events wait in its queue; excess events are dropped and counted in dropped . A looping clip emits a marker again each time playback crosses it. player.hooks uses the same fixed four-slot subscription API and reports each crossed marker as an event notice, including markers dropped from the poll queue. Skeletal players do not emit blend phases. Root translation on bone 0 is extracted as motion. rootMotionDelta() returns the displacement from the most recent update, including loop wraps; apply it to the owning entity. Use poseWithoutRootMotion() when drawing that entity, so the root's accumulated translation is not applied a second time. The player points into the data, so the data must outlive it. skeleton.BlendTree blends a sorted set of BlendNode { threshold, animation } entries as a one-dimensional blend space. BlendTree.init(&data, &nodes) rejects empty trees, non-finite or unordered thresholds, invalid durations, and animations from another data set. tree.evaluate(parameter, phase, &pose) clamps the parameter to the endpoint clips or interpolates between the adjacent clips; phase is normalized time from zero to one and each clip is sampled at the same phase. Bone positions and scales are linear blends, and rotations use the shortest angular path. This API is allocation-free; the caller owns the node array and advances the normalized phase. skeleton.place(bone, attachment) returns one attachment's rectangle, origin, and rotation in the pose's pixels. The renderer's engine.skeleton draw.drawPose(batch, texture, data, pose, sheet x, sheet y, x, y, tint, alpha) queues every attachment through SpriteBatch.drawSprite . The pivot stays on its bone, and the sprite turns with the bone. Version 1 has these limits. Keys interpolate linearly, and scale is uniform. Blend trees are one-dimensional; the caller advances their normalized phase. Root motion is extracted from the first bone's translation track. There is no inverse kinematics. Attachments have no tint, flip, or draw order of their own, so they draw in file order. The warrior and the sample game do not use skeletons yet.

title: Asset streaming
text: Asset streaming The texture store supports prioritized preloading, background decode, bounded in-flight staging, and a GPU-memory budget. Textures needed immediately can still be acquired synchronously; preloading lets the runtime do CPU work ahead of demand. The runtime starts requested loads between frames. Requests are serviced high to low priority, with registration order breaking ties. Image files are read and decoded on worker threads into staging memory; GPU upload and installation happen on the main thread. At most four decode/upload jobs are in flight, and Config.texture loads per frame caps uploads per frame. Set it to zero to disable background preloading. Config.worker threads controls the shared worker pool; zero runs jobs synchronously on the main thread. Config.texture staging budget bytes bounds the sum of decoded/compressed payloads held by in-flight loads until upload. Its default is 128 MiB; zero removes the cap. A texture larger than the entire budget fails explicitly. If a texture fits the budget but not the currently available portion, its request is deferred and retried at its original priority after staged payloads are uploaded or discarded. Streamer.stagedBytes() and each pump's deferred count expose current use and temporary pressure. The cap applies to retained payloads, not source-file read buffers or temporary decoder internals. Config.texture budget bytes sets the resident texture-cache budget. Loaded textures are estimated at four bytes per texel. When a new texture exceeds the budget, the least-recently-used unreferenced textures are evicted first. A texture with a live handle is never evicted, so the budget can temporarily be exceeded while all candidates are in use. Call ctx.releaseTexture when a handle is no longer needed, then ctx.unloadUnusedTextures if immediate reclamation is desired. ctx.textureStats() reports resident bytes, loaded count, evictions, and budget pressure. The lower-level generic asset Store(T) also exposes request , pump , setBudget , beginLoad , finishLoad , and failLoad . Those operations let a store keep cache bookkeeping on its owning thread while a caller performs a thread-safe CPU load elsewhere. GPU resources must still be created and destroyed on the graphics-owning thread. Workers must use a thread-safe allocator and must not access the store, game state, GPU, or logger. The current asynchronous pipeline is for textures. Other asset types can use the generic store's split-load interface when their loader and ownership rules support background work.

title: Streamed audio
text: Streamed audio Long sounds, such as music and ambience, can play from disk without being read into memory. Short effects still load whole with Context.loadSound , because they start at once and can be positioned without any file access during play. Using it openStreamed takes the same relative path as loadSound , and it prefers the build-encoded IMA sidecar ( music/theme.wav.ima ) when one exists, as loadSound does. playStreamed takes the same PlayOptions as play : gain, bus, loop, pan, and an optional position for a positional sound. Stop a voice with stop , and check it with isPlaying , as for any other voice. The audio system has engine.audio.max voices voice slots. When all are occupied, play and playStreamed return error.NoFreeVoice ; stop or wait for a voice rather than relying on a silent drop. Every voice uses its own gain multiplied by its bus gain and the master gain. The fixed buses are .music , .sfx , .ambience , and .ui , each defaulting to gain 1. Set one with audio.setBusGain(.music, 0.5) ; this applies immediately to already-playing voices on that bus. Gains clamp to [0, 1] , and non-finite gains become zero. PlayOptions.bus defaults to .sfx ; choose .music for a music stream or .ambience for an ambience loop. The master gain remains the overall volume control. A StreamedSound holds only the path and the format. It owns no file and needs no deinit . Each playing voice opens its own reader, which closes when the voice ends or is stopped. The same StreamedSound can play several times at once. What is held in memory A loaded sound queues its whole length. A streamed voice that is not positional keeps one second of converted sound queued instead, so a hitch in the game loop of up to a second does not reach the output. A positional streamed voice keeps the same short lookahead as a positional loaded sound, a tenth of a second, so moving it is heard promptly. Each read fills at most 4096 bytes, and an IMA read decodes at most 1024 frames, into one buffer that all voices share. Formats - WAV: PCM at 8, 16, or 32 bits, and IEEE float at 32 bits. Extensible WAV is accepted when its sub-format is one of these. 24-bit and other formats are refused with UnsupportedFormat , and loadSound still plays them. A data chunk longer than the file is clipped to the bytes present. - BRAD IMA ADPCM (the build's .ima sidecar): mono or stereo. The sidecar stores each channel as a whole block, so a chunk reads a run of nibbles from each block at its own offset. The decoder is checked sample for sample against the whole-file decoder in audio/ima.zig . Sound converts from its own rate and channel count to the device's format through an SDL stream that keeps its resampling state between chunks, so a sound cut into chunks sounds the same as one converted whole. Looping A looping streamed voice starts its sound again at the end. Its converter keeps running across the join, so the loop has no gap at the seam. A voice that cannot read its sound any further stops looping and finishes once its queued sound has played out, so a read error never leaves a silent voice running forever. Files and the platform platform/sdl/files.zig provides open , close , size , and readAt for reads at chosen offsets. platform/sdl/audio.zig provides createConverter and getStreamData . Both sit behind platform.zig , so audio/streaming.zig and audio/audio.zig keep their SDL-free boundary. audio/streaming.zig reads only through a Source (a context, a read function, and a size), so its tests run with no device and no file system. Not covered yet - Streaming from a file that changes while a voice plays. The reader trusts the size it read when the voice started. - Music that is decoded ahead on a worker thread. Each chunk is decoded on the main thread, which is cheap for these formats.

title: Build profiles
text: Build profiles Use -Dprofile= to select a named preset. development is the default. The profile sets the default optimization mode and the defaults for development tools and GPU validation; explicit options can override those defaults. Profile Optimization Development tools GPU validation Intended use --- --- --- --- --- development Debug On Off Normal local work: overlay, diagnostics, console, and hot reload debug Debug Off On Minimal runtime with Debug checks and SDL GPU validation release ReleaseFast Off Off Packaged player builds Assertions and the default log threshold follow Zig's optimization mode, not the profile name. Debug and ReleaseSafe check assertions and default to debug logs; ReleaseFast and ReleaseSmall compile assertions out and default to info logs. The settings file can still override the runtime log threshold. Examples -Doptimize , -Ddev-tools , and -Dgpu-debug override the corresponding profile defaults. Bare --release selects ReleaseFast ; an explicit -Doptimize takes precedence. Tracy, DXIL, and Metal remain opt-in, orthogonal build features. -Ddxil=true and -Dmetal=true embed additional shader targets; they do not force the runtime to select that backend. The release script builds with the release profile unless -Profile selects another preset. With -SkipBuild , the script packages existing files and records the selected profile as supplied by the caller; it cannot verify how those files were compiled.

title: Developer command console
text: Developer command console The console is available only when development tools are enabled. In Debug builds, press F2 to open/close it. Text is collected through SDL text input; Enter submits, Backspace edits, and Escape closes it. The console uses fixed-size input/output buffers and does not evaluate expressions or access files, memory, or code. Command Purpose --- --- help List registered commands scene Show the scene hierarchy: open scenes from the root to the active one, the switch count, and any pending transition entities Show the published entity count assets Show texture cache counts and estimated bytes performance Show average, p95, and maximum frame time plus phase averages performance PHASE Inspect frame , events , asset , update , audio , draw , or present tile Show the ground tile and collision metadata under the cursor diagnostics on\ off\ toggle Show or hide the diagnostics overlay collision on\ off\ toggle Toggle collision visualization tiles on\ off\ toggle Toggle tile-boundary visualization layer NAME on\ off\ toggle Show/hide ground , decoration , or foreground Commands are explicitly registered in engine/diagnostics/console.zig . Arguments are checked strictly; unknown commands and invalid arguments return usage text. Commands read the published diagnostics snapshot or change only supported diagnostic visibility switches. The parser and registry are pure and covered by zig build test . Build with zig build run -Ddev-tools=false to omit the console and other development services. Release builds have development tools disabled by default.

title: 2D lighting
text: 2D lighting The sprite batch supports ambient and point lighting for lit sprites. A sprite uses a normal map through Options.normal , or the flat, viewer-facing normal with Options.lit = true . Each frame, set the ambient RGB and add point lights and optional shadow segments to the batch before queuing the lit sprites: Light and shadow coordinates are in view pixels, matching sprite positions after camera projection. addShadowSegment defines a 2D line segment: for each lit fragment, it blocks a point light when the segment lies between the fragment and the light. The light's contribution is omitted behind the segment; ambient illumination remains. This produces hard 2D shadows. Segments are supplied per frame and are not inferred from tile or sprite geometry. Normal maps are selected with Options.normal ; .lit = true uses the batch-owned flat viewer-facing normal for a sprite without a normal map. Normal maps must match the albedo texture dimensions. Sprite flip and rotation also transform the normal map basis in the lit shader. The public ECS-friendly types PointLightComponent and ShadowSegmentComponent can be accumulated directly by the batch: The world form supports dense AoS or SoA rows containing the named component fields. Each enabled component is accumulated for the current frame. Slices can be supplied with addPointLightComponents and addShadowSegmentComponents . A batch supports up to engine.max lights point lights and engine.max shadow segments shadow segments per frame. addLight and addShadowSegment return false when full; the component-slice and world helpers return the number accepted, skipping entries after capacity. begin resets ambient to full brightness and clears the lights and segments, so configure them for each frame. Unlit sprites are unaffected.

title: Localization
text: Localization The public bairava.localization module provides locale identifiers and an in-memory translation catalog. Create a catalog with a required fallback locale, register other locales, add translations, and select the active locale: Locale tags are case-insensitive ASCII alphanumeric subtags separated by single hyphens and are normalized to lowercase ( fr-CA becomes fr-ca ). The fallback locale is registered by Catalog.init ; other locales must be registered before translations can be added or selected. Lookup checks the active locale first, then the fallback locale. If neither has a translation, lookup returns null . Translation keys follow the engine's validated-name rules: lowercase names containing letters, digits, , - , and . , with optional / -separated segments. Translation values are copied into the catalog's owned storage. Repeated locale IDs and translation keys return error.Duplicate ; lookups do not allocate.

title: Logging and diagnostic error reporting
text: Logging and diagnostic error reporting Status: P2.3. Levels From least to most severe: trace , debug , info , warn , error . A message below the minimum level is dropped before it is formatted. The minimum starts at debug in Debug builds and at info in the other modes. Choosing the level in the settings file log level = debug Accepted values are trace , debug , info , warn (or warning ), and error , in any case. A value that is not a level name is logged and the default is kept. The setting is read at startup, before the window opens, so startup messages honor it. Release builds use the same setting, so a shipped build can log more when a tester sets it. Writing messages const log = engine.log.scoped("game"); log.trace("per-step detail", .{}); log.info("level loaded: {s}", .{name}); Each line carries a scope, which names the subsystem. Use the scope of the module that owns the work. Failures Every failure says three things: the operation, the resource it was working on, and the error. - engine.log.recovered(scope, operation, resource, err, instead) logs a warning, for a failure the caller continues past. The last argument says what happens instead. Example: a missing debug font logs that the overlay is off. - engine.log.fatal(scope, operation, resource, err) logs an error, for a failure that stops the operation. The caller then returns the error. Neither helper replaces the error. The caller still returns the typed Zig error it received, so callers can still match on it. Startup failures Session.start records the step it is on. If a step fails, the run logs one summary line naming the subsystem and the operation: startup failed in the window subsystem while creating the window: WindowCreateFailed; anything opened before it was released Startup failures are fatal: the run returns the error, and the caller decides the exit status. Cleanup still happens in reverse order through errdefer , as docs/ownership.md describes. The unit tests cover the stage names and the summary text. Testing the teardown itself needs a window and a GPU device, so it is covered by review. Recoverable and fatal, in short Situation Level Stops the run? --- --- --- Missing optional file (a sidecar, a font for the overlay) debug or warn, via recovered No Asset that fails to load, where the game can fall back warn, via recovered No Save that fails to write error, via fatal No, the game keeps running Engine startup step fails error, the summary line Yes Broken invariant assertion panic (Debug, ReleaseSafe) Yes Log file The log file ( Semkootru.log , beside the executable) takes the same levels as the terminal. Every line is flushed as it is written, so the file is complete even after a crash. Each run replaces the previous file. The C sink maps trace to LOG TRACE in log.c, and it clamps any level outside 0 to 4. Crash reports A panic writes a crash report beside the executable, as Semkootru.crash.txt , before Zig prints the stack trace. The report holds the panic message, the frame number, the scene name, the mouse position in window points, and the held keys. Each run removes the report left by the run before it, at startup, so a report always belongs to the run that wrote it. The stack trace goes to the terminal only. The frame loop records the frame, scene, and input once per frame with a few stores. That happens in every build, so a release crash has the same context as a debug one. The game sets the report file name with crash file in its config. Null writes no report, and the log still records the panic. Not done - No log rotation, and no logs kept from earlier runs. Both are listed as open items in the README. - No third-party logging framework.

title: Navigation
text: Navigation Navigation lets AI units find routes through a level. It has two parts. The engine provides the walkable grid, the route search, and a follower that walks a box along a route through the tile map's collision. The sample game uses those parts to wander, chase the player, and walk home. The engine modules name no game type. The public namespace is exported through engine.navigation ; its navigation module collects the grid, pathfinder, follower, agent, and flow-field APIs. The enemy state machine and game-specific movement remain in the sample game. The walkable grid navigation.Grid wraps a TileMap . A cell is walkable when the map does not block it. A solid tile on any layer blocks its cell, and the edge of the map counts as a wall. A grid keeps a pointer to its map, so make one where it is used, and don't store it in a struct that is later moved. One-way tile cells remain walkable and do not block line of sight. A rejects only a southward step into a one-way cell; northward and sideways entry remain available. cellOf gives the cell that holds a point in pixels, and cellCenter gives the center of a cell. Grid.lineOfSight answers whether a straight line between two points crosses only walkable cells. It checks every cell the line crosses, in order, so it cannot step past a thin wall at a corner. Grid.perceive(from, to, sight) filters finite points by an optional pixel range and facing cone before calling the same line-of-sight walk. The default Sight is unlimited and omnidirectional, so it behaves like lineOfSight for finite points. One-way tiles remain transparent to sight because only solid cells block the walk. The engine takes a direction vector rather than a game-facing enum; callers map their own facing to world-space x/y. Routes navigation.Pathfinder runs A over the grid, and returns the cheapest route as a list of cells, from start to goal. - A route may enter a cell from any of its eight neighbors. A straight step costs 10, and a diagonal step costs 14. - A diagonal step is allowed only when both cells beside it are walkable. A route never squeezes between two wall corners. - The start may be inside a wall, since a unit can be pushed there. The goal must be walkable. - find writes the route into a buffer the caller provides. A failed search writes nothing, so the caller's old route stays in place. The errors are OutOfBounds , GoalBlocked , NoPath , and PathTooLong . - The pathfinder keeps its arrays between searches, and only grows them when a bigger map is searched. A search can visit every cell of the map, so its worst case grows with the map. Enemies keep the cost low: a chasing unit can instead share a flow field with all other units chasing the same cell. Shared-goal flow fields navigation.FlowField runs Dijkstra backward from one or more walkable goal cells. It stores a cost-to-goal for each reachable cell and, after the costs settle, one legal neighbor with a lower cost. nextCell(grid, cell) samples that direction without running another search. One-way entry and diagonal corner rules use the same step legality and 10/14 costs as A . Build the field when its shared goal changes. buildGoals can seed several destinations; a failed build caused by an empty, blocked, or out-of-bounds goal leaves the previous field intact. Unreachable cells and goal cells return no next cell. The field has no route-length limit, and A remains available for unique destinations. Follower.stepToward moves a box toward one pixel-space waypoint using the same tile collision, 2 px arrival snap, and 0.35 second stuck handling as route following. This is the intended movement step for a unit sampling a flow field; it does not allocate or retain a cell route. Navigation agent navigation.Agent composes a reusable A pathfinder and route follower for one moving unit. Initialize it with an allocator, call plan(grid, start, goal) , then pass the map, the unit's collision box, speed, and fixed update delta to step . goal , hasPath , atGoal , and nextWaypoint expose the current route state. clear drops both the route and its remembered goal. The agent owns its pathfinder, so call deinit when it is no longer needed. Planning is transactional: if a new goal is blocked, unreachable, outside the grid, too far for the route buffer, or allocation fails, the current route remains available and plan returns the error. The caller chooses when to replan for moving targets or changed world state. The map and grid remain caller-owned; the map must outlive each step . Following a route navigation.Follower holds a route of up to max path (128) cells. Its step moves a box toward the next waypoint, by at most speed dt pixels. The box uses the same collision as the player, so it slides along walls and stops where a solid tile blocks it. When the box comes within 2 pixels of an open waypoint, it snaps onto that cell's center. Steering diagonally can leave the box a fraction of a pixel off the grid, and that fraction can put its edge over a wall row, which then blocks the next straight move. Snapping keeps the box on the grid. A box centered on an open cell never overlaps a wall. If the box makes no progress for 0.35 seconds while it still has a route, the follower drops the route. The owner decides what to do next, and a chasing enemy replans on its next repath. Enemies The sample game's enemy brain uses four states and the game code plans and walks the enemy. State Entered when What it does Leaves when --- --- --- --- idle at spawn, or after a rest stands still for a random 1.5 to 3.0 seconds sees the player: chase. Wait over: wander wander the idle wait ends routes to a random walkable cell within 4 cells of home sees the player: chase. Route done: idle chase sees the player, from any state samples the shared field toward the player's cell at 44 pixels per second no sight for 2.0 seconds: return home return home lost sight of the player routes back to home, at 20 pixels per second sees the player: chase. Arrived: idle An enemy sees the player when the player's feet are within 88 pixels of its own feet, and a clear line joins them. Walls block sight. Enemies don't see each other, and they don't attack yet. Each enemy is drawn with the warrior's walk and idle clips, tinted red. Its brain is seeded from its position in the level's list, so every run of a level makes the same random choices. Enemies are placed with enemy lines in the level's metadata file. The cell is the enemy's home. See [prefabs](prefabs.html) for the file format. Changing the numbers The sample's speeds, sight range, wander radius, repath interval, idle wait, and lose-sight time are game choices. The navigation system's route step costs, arrival distance, and stuck timeout are engine behavior. Debugging - F4 turns on the debug geometry. Each enemy's feet are outlined in red, and the cells left on its route are drawn as blue points. - In development builds, the debug overlay (F3) lists the enemy count and how many are chasing. Tests zig build test runs the grid, pathfinder, flow field, follower, navigation agent, and behavior brain tests. The repository's sample game is also compiled as part of the normal build. Limits - Enemies do not fight, and the player takes no damage. - Enemies are not saved. Loading a save leaves them on their home cells, as the level placed them. - An A route holds at most 128 cells. A longer one is refused with PathTooLong ; flow-field steering has no route length limit. - Enemies do not avoid each other or the player, so they can overlap. - The grid is built from the static tiles of the level. A route does not change when a tile changes. - Routes are not smoothed. A route can zigzag between diagonal and straight steps.

title: Particles
text: Particles bairava.particles.System simulates bounded, deterministic particles and can queue them as sprites. Create a system with an allocator, maximum live-particle count, and RNG seed; configure it, set its emitter position, then call update(dt) during game updates: Continuous emission preserves fractional particles between updates. emit(count) creates a burst immediately and returns the number that fit; the system never exceeds its fixed capacity and does not allocate after initialization. Particle lifetime, speed, angle, and size ranges are sampled deterministically from the supplied seed. setConfig rejects non-finite or out-of-range values without changing the previous configuration. Non-finite and non-positive update steps are ignored. To draw, call System.draw(&sprite batch, texture, source rect, z, camera) after beginning the sprite batch. Particles are centered on their positions and interpolate their size and RGBA tint over their lifetime. Drawing culls each particle against the camera's world-space view, including the particle's rotation and a one-pixel pad for camera rounding. Gravity is constant per system and affects velocity. Game code owns the texture and controls particle-system lifetime.

title: Physics and collision queries
text: Physics and collision queries The engine provides SDL-free shape and collision helpers in engine.physics . Shapes and colliders Collider and collision.Component support a box or optional circle shape, one or more collision layers, a query mask, and an enabled flag. Box colliders may be rotated or marked one way . Components can be attached to dense ECS rows and copied into collider slices with collision.collidersFromWorld . Rotation is stored in radians and turns clockwise around the rectangle's center in screen space. Collider half-open edges follow box semantics: right and bottom edges are outside the shape. An axis-aligned collider with one way = true blocks only downward movement at its top edge. Horizontal and upward movement pass through it. A rotated collider remains a full block even when flagged one-way. Set circle to use a circle as the collider's only shape; the box and rotation fields are then ignored. A null circle preserves the box behavior. Circles are open disks: rim contact is not an overlap. A circle ignores one way and blocks movement as a solid shape in every direction. Set is trigger = true to make a collider a sensor. Triggers remain in overlap, point, region, and grid queries, but are ignored by box movement response. Detection orientedBoxesOverlap uses the separating-axis theorem for exact rectangle-vs-rectangle overlap. circleOverlapsBox , circlesOverlap , and pointInCircle provide the corresponding strict circle tests. These operations do not allocate and do not report movement. queries.firstOverlap , anyOverlap , queryRegion , and firstAtPoint operate on collider slices. Every operation filters disabled colliders and checks the collision layer/mask relationship. queries.collectTriggerEvents compares current trigger overlaps with a caller-owned previous-pair slice and fills caller-owned current-pair and event buffers. It emits enter , stay , and exit events for pairs where at least one enabled collider is a trigger. Pairwise layer/mask checks apply, indices are ordered by the collider slice, and that slice must keep the same ordering across updates. The result reports total pair/event counts and how many entries did not fit in either output buffer; size those buffers for the expected maximum if every pair and event must be retained. Use the current pair buffer as the previous-pair slice on the next fixed update. Rays and shape casts queries.raycast returns the nearest Hit along a segment; raycastAll writes hits sorted by fraction and then collider index, retaining the nearest hits when its output is too small. Both include trigger colliders and filter disabled colliders by layer mask. Box faces count as contact surfaces (including the otherwise-exclusive right and bottom edges), and circle tangencies count as hits. A ray that starts inside a shape returns fraction zero with an outward normal; a zero-length ray therefore only hits when its origin is inside (or on a box contact face; circle containment is strict). Empty or non-finite geometry and ray inputs miss. queries.castBox sweeps an axis-aligned box and queries.castCircle sweeps a circle. Their Hit point is the moving shape's reference position at first contact (box top-left or circle center). The uniform-grid Index provides matching raycast , raycastAll , castBox , and castCircle queries over its static collider slice. Uniform grid broad phase.Index stores static colliders in a uniform grid. Rebuild the index after collider data changes. Rotated colliders are inserted using their conservative axis-aligned bounding box; candidate boxes and points then use exact SAT or oriented-point checks. The index supports region, overlap, point, and movement queries. queries.moveBoxIgnoringOneWay and Index.moveBoxIgnoringOneWay provide a one-slide drop-through operation. They skip axis-aligned one-way tops while retaining solid and rotated-collider response. Movement Linear and grid movement resolve X before Y, preserve movement that starts inside an overlapping collider as escape movement, and stop at blockers when exact overlap first appears. Rotated candidates use exact narrow-phase overlap checks, and circle colliders use analytic box-to-circle contact stops. The moving probe remains a box. One-way response is optional and does not change existing colliders: the default one way = false keeps them fully solid. The movement implementation is axis-based: it does not rotate the moving box. Swept rotated-box response, complete rotated shape resolution, and rotation of the mover are outside the current requirement.

title: Prefabs
text: Prefabs Prefabs are named entity templates. The game's prefab file defines them, and the level metadata places them by name. Each placement spawns one entity in the game's ECS world, and the entity draws its prefab's tile. The prefab file assets/prefabs.txt holds one statement per line. starts a comment, and blank lines are ignored. - prefab starts a template. A name uses lowercase letters, digits, and , and is at most 32 bytes. - tile names the tile the template draws: an index into the level's tileset, counted left to right and then down, the same as the tile layers. Each template needs exactly one tile line. Any other line is an error. The file holds at most 64 templates. Level metadata assets/maps/level1.spawn holds the level's game metadata. It has one spawn line, and any number of place and enemy lines: - spawn is the cell where the player starts. It is required, and it appears once. - place spawns one entity from the named template on that cell. A level holds at most 4096 placements. - enemy starts one enemy on that cell, and the cell is its home. Enemies wander near it, chase the player when they can see it, and walk home after losing it. A level holds at most 64 enemies. See [navigation](navigation.html). The file keeps its .spawn name for now, although it also holds placements and enemies. Checks - zig build check-assets parses the prefab file, and checks the level metadata against the map's size and the prefab names. The metadata must depend on the game prefabs asset in assets/asset manifest.txt . - At startup the game checks that every prefab's tile exists in the tileset, and it stops if one does not. An atlas reload that would break a prefab's tile is rejected, and the current atlas stays in use. - Unknown prefab names, cells outside the map, and malformed lines are all errors. Limits - The only component is tile . A placed entity draws its tile and blocks nothing, so the player walks through it. - Placed entities and enemies are not saved. Loading the level spawns them again from the metadata. - The prefab file and the level metadata are read at startup only. Edits take effect after a restart. - The example marker tile is a placeholder. It was chosen for contrast with the ground, not for its art.

title: Profiling and repeatable workload
text: Profiling and repeatable workload Development builds retain 120 frame samples per phase. The diagnostics overlay reports average, nearest-rank p95, and worst frame time; performance in the F2 console prints the same summaries with update, draw, and present phase averages. Timed phases are frame, event processing, asset watcher polling, fixed update, audio maintenance, world draw/submission, and presentation. Asset reload work performed inside the game's update remains part of update timing. Run the deterministic rendering workload with: It updates 10,000 simple moving game entities, rebuilds a collision grid for their moving colliders, performs 1,000 region queries per fixed update, and draws one tinted sprite per entity from one 4x4 texture at a 320x180 native view. Entities start in a fixed 100-by-100 grid and wrap horizontally; the workload and texture are the same each run and use no random state or dynamic spawning. Use the same build mode, resolution, vsync setting, and graphics backend when comparing results. Let it run past its 60-frame warm-up and the 120 frames it summarizes, then record average, p95, and worst frame times along with the individual phase averages. F3 toggles the overlay; F2 opens the console, where performance prints the current summary; Escape quits. Run the typography reference workload with: It draws the authored bitmap font, BFNT coverage, runtime-shaped Latin and Tamil, and MSDF from the same native 320x180 view. Use F10 to compare SDL GPU with SDL3 2D; Escape quits. After its 60-frame warm-up and 120-frame sample window, it logs frame average/p95, shaping and measure time, cache hits and misses, rasterized glyphs, atlas pages and CPU bytes, upload regions/bytes, and draw calls. The timings are local to the loaded font workload. Capture screenshots on a display for visual review; the log is profiling evidence, not screenshot acceptance. At shutdown, the engine also reports cumulative shaping, cache, atlas upload, and retirement counts. Those counters are useful for diagnosing a run but are not a machine-independent performance baseline. For cold/warm comparisons, use the reference workload and record its machine and backend details as above. The measurements are deliberately runtime-local and are not uploaded. No machine-independent baseline is committed because results depend on hardware, drivers, window compositor, and vsync. Record the machine/OS, CPU/GPU, Zig version, build mode, backend, and workload count beside any captured measurements. The overlay's counters include sprites/draw submissions, the game's published entity count, texture-cache counts/estimated bytes, and gameplay-published collision query calls. -Dtracy=true additionally enables Tracy zones for function-level investigation. Compare the repeatable workload first and use those zones to locate a measured bottleneck before changing data layouts or caches. The benchmark also logs that summary itself, under the benchmark log scope, once the warm-up and 120 frames are recorded. It reports cumulative collision query calls and hits as well. The benchmark turns on Config.gpu timing , so it logs the GPU summary too, and it logs the spike count with it. Its frame figures therefore include the GPU wait. It runs only in development builds, where the frame times are kept, so a release build logs nothing. The overlay shows a strip of allocations per frame and a line of per-frame plot values. The plots are sprites queued, draw calls made last frame, allocations requested so far this frame across every scope, and bytes requested. Each plot keeps the same 120-frame window as the frame graph, so its average and p95 are over those frames. Allocation counts restart at the start of each frame, while the totals in the memory line keep counting from startup. -Dtracy=true also sends those four plots to Tracy, and it draws them beside the zones. The plot calls use Tracy's C entry point tracy emit plot . If a Tracy build fails to link on that name, check the Tracy headers in the vendored tree. GPU time is measured only when Config.gpu timing is set, and the benchmark sets it. The engine then submits each frame and waits on a fence until the GPU finishes it. That wait is the gpu phase, it is the last part of present , and it is sent to Tracy as the gpu ms plot. The pass zones still measure only the CPU's recording work. SDL's GPU API, as this engine uses it, does not appear to expose timestamp queries, so the figure covers the whole frame and not each pass. Confirm this against the pinned SDL version before relying on it. The wait stalls the CPU, so with gpu timing on the CPU and GPU work add up. Those frame times measure a cost, not a rate to play at, and they should not be compared with a run that leaves the option off. A frame longer than two 60 Hz budgets (33 ms) is a spike. The overlay shows how many have happened since startup, and the latest one with its frame count and the phase that took most of that frame. Spikes are recorded only in development builds.

title: Deterministic input replay and state checkpoints
text: Deterministic input replay and state checkpoints The fixed-step loop gives every simulation update the same dt . engine.replay.Log records the input snapshot seen by each update and reapplies those snapshots without consulting platform input. The game owns the log and chooses where to record or play it: For playback, replace live input immediately before the update: recordInput requires consecutive ticks. seek positions the playback cursor at an exact recorded tick, and rewind restarts it. A replayed input includes held keys, key press/release edges, mouse state and position, gamepad identities, axes, held controls, and gamepad edges. Platform events are not replayed; gameplay should use the recorded input snapshot and deterministic simulation state rather than live device state. The engine cannot serialize arbitrary game state, so games provide their own stable snapshot representation: After restoring, advance by repeatedly applying applyNextInput and running one fixed update, until the desired tick. Context.simulation tick is a zero-based fixed-update index. recordInput records the snapshot visible during that update. A checkpoint's tick denotes the next update boundary to run; record the initial state at tick zero and record the state after update N at tick N + 1. Checkpoints are copied into the log and carry a checksum. The nearest checkpoint at or before a target tick can be restored; restoreStateAtOrBefore checks the checksum and output capacity. Snapshots must be recorded in increasing tick order. Use the same game version, initial content, fixed update rate, and deterministic random seeds for a meaningful replay. The log is currently an in-memory runtime facility; persistence and cross-version compatibility are the game's responsibility. Replays do not make nondeterministic game code deterministic by themselves. Simulation must avoid wall-clock reads, unordered iteration, and unseeded randomness, and must define how external events are handled.

title: Text and fonts
text: Text and fonts Game code uses one text surface: load a FontHandle , then measure, lay out, and draw through Canvas.text , Canvas.textWidth , Canvas.layoutText , and Canvas.drawTextLayout . The font provider and renderer-specific texture details stay inside the engine. The compatibility text methods use HarfBuzz's Latn / en defaults. For scripts that need explicit shaping properties, pass ui.TextOptions to Canvas.textWithOptions , Canvas.textWidthWithOptions , and Canvas.layoutTextWithOptions , for example .{ .script = "Taml", .language = "ta" } . Measurement and layout must use the same options as drawing so widths, wrapping, and glyph placement agree. These options affect runtime outline and MSDF fonts; static BFNT and bitmap providers retain their existing codepoint-based behavior. There are three rendering kinds: Kind Source and loading Sampling and rendering --- --- --- Static coverage BFNT is baked offline; hand-authored BMFont bitmap descriptors are also accepted as a coverage provider. BFNT uses Context.loadFont(path, pixel height) . Bitmap fonts use Context.loadBitmapFont(path) and the size recorded by the descriptor. GPU uses R8 coverage; SDL3 2D uses the matching white-RGBA/alpha texture. Nearest filtering and whole-pixel placement preserve pixel edges. Runtime coverage TrueType glyf outlines loaded with Context.loadOutlineFont(path, pixel height) . pixel height fixes the face size. Glyphs are rasterized on demand into the session's bounded coverage atlas. GPU and SDL3 2D use the shared dynamic coverage pages, synchronized before drawing. Sampling is nearest. MSDF An offline MFNT v1 asset generated from a TrueType source; load with Context.loadMsdfFont(path, pixel height) . The baked pixel height must match. pxRange is stored in the descriptor; the current baker uses 4. SDL GPU uses the median-distance shader and a per-texture clamp-to-edge linear sampler. SDL3 2D uses the matching coverage sibling, not the RGB distance field. Hand-authored bitmap fonts are a distinct import/metrics provider, but share the static coverage rendering path; they are not converted to MSDF. The existing .bfnt format remains supported through its compatibility adapter. Asset pipeline An ordinary BFNT manifest row bakes an atlas and metrics at one size: The final optional field selects gray or mono rasterization. BFNT v4 records a fallback codepoint; older BFNT v1/v2 files retain their documented compatibility defaults. BFNT v3, which carried the old signed-distance flag, is rejected. Hand-authored bitmap fonts use a coverage row to package each grayscale PNG page as tightly packed .r8 bytes, plus a bitmap font row for the AngelCode BMFont descriptor. The source descriptor names PNG basenames; the packaged descriptor names the matching .r8 basenames. Pages use nearest sampling, authored rectangles and offsets, and integer placement/scaling. Bitmap mapping is one glyph per UTF-8 codepoint with authored kerning and a descriptor fallback. It does not provide ligatures or complex-script shaping. An MSDF row uses the msdf mode and outputs a separate .mfnt asset. The offline asset builder runs msdfgen over supported outlines and emits both the RGBA MSDF atlas and an R8 coverage sibling. The atlas cap is 1024×1024 per font: 4 MiB MSDF plus 1 MiB coverage. Oversized bakes fail; glyphs are not dropped and the atlas does not grow. Use the same baked size when loading BFNT or MFNT. Runtime outline faces are initialized at their requested pixel height ; they are not silently resized later. A bitmap font's size comes from its descriptor. pxRange is an MSDF distance-field parameter, not a font size or a scale multiplier. Shaping, fallback, and limits Runtime outline and MSDF fonts use HarfBuzz shaping with explicit script, language, and direction. The compatibility defaults are Latn , en , and left-to-right. Horizontal LTR text is supported; paragraph bidi processing is not. Runtime outlines accept TrueType glyf outlines; CFF/CFF2 and TrueType collections are unsupported for that path. There is no font fallback chain. A missing runtime cmap entry or .notdef glyph resolves once, after shaping, to ? in that same face; if the face has no ? , no ink is drawn. BFNT and bitmap fonts use their recorded/descriptor fallback when available and otherwise draw nothing for the missing glyph. Coverage textures, including BFNT and bitmap pages, stay nearest-filtered. MSDF atlases alone get a clamp-to-edge linear sampler; changing that sampler does not change pixel-art or other textures. MSDF requires the GPU median shader for distance-field reconstruction. The SDL3 2D backend cannot run that shader and therefore draws the coverage sibling baked from the same source. It never displays the raw RGB distance field. The existing C BFNT code remains only as a compatibility adapter. It is not a second public text API, and no legacy BFNT consumer or asset format is removed by this migration. Resource lifetime and diagnostics CPU atlas bytes remain owned by BFNT, bitmap, MSDF, and runtime-coverage resources so their text GPU textures can be rebuilt after an idle-safe resource reset while the device is still valid. The engine does not currently expose a full SDL GPU device-loss recovery/replacement path; retaining pixels alone does not imply that the whole renderer can survive device loss. Unloaded font handles become stale immediately. Their GPU resources remain alive while queued work may refer to them, and are collected at an idle-safe point. Runtime atlas uploads remain pending until the frame command buffer submits successfully; staging or submission failures are surfaced and retried. SDL's coverage upload call has no per-copy result, so the engine cannot reliably detect an individual copy failure through that API. Run zig build run-text-benchmark for a deterministic bitmap/BFNT/Latin/Tamil/MSDF scene and text-specific shaping, cache, atlas, upload, draw-call, and frame counters. Its output supplements but does not replace display-backed visual acceptance. Validation and visual acceptance zig build test runs the engine, C UI, and asset-tool tests. zig build test-ui runs the C text and widget tests directly, and zig build check-assets validates manifests and packaged assets. The asset builder tests cover bitmap, BFNT, and MFNT generation, including malformed inputs and the MSDF size cap. Visual acceptance still requires reference captures for the mono bitmap font, gray BFNT, shaped Latin, shaped Tamil (vowel signs and conjuncts), and MSDF at native and enlarged scales. Compare coverage aliasing with MSDF smoothness, verify the median shader on SDL GPU and the coverage sibling on SDL3 2D, and confirm an ordinary non-font texture remains nearest-filtered. These are display-backed checks; successful compilation or CPU tests alone do not close them.

title: Runtime platform capabilities
text: Runtime platform capabilities Games can query the active runtime through Context.capabilities() . It returns the SDL-independent engine.Capabilities value and is valid only while the engine is running. GPU results reflect both formats embedded in this build and formats accepted by the active GPU device. audio playback reports whether the default playback device opened, and presentation.immediate reports whether the active window supports immediate presentation without vsync. shader formats reports SPIR-V, DXIL, and MSL support only when both the vertex and fragment shaders are embedded and the GPU accepts that format. texture formats reports RGBA8 and the optional BC1, BC3, and ASTC 4x4 sampling formats. RGBA8 is the engine's required uncompressed fallback. Unsupported-feature behavior - Compressed textures: the asset loader tries supported ASTC, BC3, BC1, and RGBA8 variants in that order. Missing, malformed, or unsupported variants fall through to the next variant, then decode the original image as RGBA8. If the original is also missing or invalid, texture loading returns an AssetError ; it does not report a successful fallback. Compression support comes from the active GPU. If renderer switching is enabled, compressed variants are disabled until every renderer can use a compatible representation. - Required GPU formats: startup fails with UnsupportedGpuCapabilities before creating renderer resources if there is no usable embedded shader format or the active device cannot sample RGBA8. Games that reach init can rely on both requirements; shader formats and texture formats.rgba8 describe the available alternatives and required baseline. - Audio playback: failure to open the default device is non-fatal and the game runs silently. audio playback is false; sound loading and playback return error.NoDevice . Audio decode and conversion helpers that operate on caller-provided data do not require a playback device. - Shader formats: only compiled formats are requested from SDL and reported as usable. The engine needs at least one format to create its renderer; otherwise startup returns UnsupportedGpuCapabilities instead of silently drawing nothing. - Immediate presentation: check caps.presentation.immediate before offering a no-vsync setting. If a configuration requests immediate presentation on a display that does not support it, the engine keeps vsync on and logs a warning. A true value means the mode is supported, not that it is currently selected. - Development-only tools: diagnostics, the overlay, console, and hot reload are controlled by the build profile and -Ddev-tools ; they are not runtime capabilities and are absent when compiled out. The capability query reports the session's current device and window. It does not promise that a later device, display, or target will have the same capabilities.

title: Public API
text: Bairava public API This reference is generated from an explicit allowlist of canonical names exported by @import("bairava") . Only allowlisted entries are published; implementation target paths are validated but never displayed. The current public API is experimental and not production-ready. 87 allowlisted exports. All entries inherit the project's experimental API status. Callable export types are emitted from compiler reflection; contract notes are authored and reviewed in the manifest. bairava.Config Kind: type Stability: experimental Summary: Application configuration, window, renderer, and runtime settings. Contract: The parent allocator must outlive the entire run. Settings-file window values override the corresponding startup values. Config.validate returns a specific error before any platform resource is opened. - Config.allocator (allocators): Parent allocator for engine, game, asset, and frame allocations; it must remain valid through the full run. If worker threads is nonzero, it must be thread-safe. - Config.window w, window h (fields): Initial native window dimensions in pixels; each must be from 64 through 8192. - Config.native w, native h (fields): Reference view dimensions in pixels.
